_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-11) the developer is now Gwenno Jewell, so her surname is not two letters from the councillor's
title: Keeping It Fresh
setting: a newspaper morgue at press time

post.author: u/press_time_morvoren
post.title: I run the night desk at a local paper. At 22:30 our archive assistant quoted me an article we deleted two years ago, and a draft I'm not allowed to read.

blocks.text: I'm the night editor at the Gullstone Herald. Press time is 23:15. Since the spring of 2024 the newsroom has had an archive assistant: you type a question, it searches the morgue and the content system, the program where we write, edit and publish everything, and a model writes the answer from the chunks it finds. Gwenno Jewell, our developer, built it. It started with a one-off load of everything on 2 April 2024, and since then it has picked up new and edited articles as they happen.
On Thursday at 22:30 a page-five story needed background on Councillor Hedley Carnsew, so I asked it.

22:30  night desk  Background on Councillor Hedley Carnsew, please.
22:30  assistant   Two sources claim Councillor Carnsew took money from the car
                    park contractor [art-1187]. He met the dredging firm's director
                    on 3 September; the meeting is not in his register of
                    interests [inv-0912].

I clicked art-1187. The content system said there is no such article. I know why. On 17 October 2024, after a legal complaint, we retracted that story, printed an apology and deleted it. I was on the desk the night it came down. The assistant quoted it word for word, and its link opened onto a page that said the article does not exist.
It remembered an article we had buried, and it wanted me to print it again.

inv-0912 is worse. It's a draft on the investigations desk, under embargo until 06:00 on Friday: nobody outside that desk may read it or act on it before then. In the content system every article and draft has access groups, the groups of staff allowed to open it. Published articles are in newsroom, which I'm in. Wylla Trewin's drafts are in investigations, which I'm not. Nobody on my desk had ever seen that sentence. Wylla created the draft at 18:12.

blocks.label: thursday_2230_sent.png

diagram.aria: Gwenno's drawing of the four chunks sent to the model at 22:30 on Thursday, by score. Rank 1, 0.91: art-1187 chunk 1, version 1, deleted 17 Oct 2024. Rank 2, 0.88: art-2290 chunk 1, version 2, live, newsroom. Rank 3, 0.86: inv-0912 chunk 1, version 1, investigations only. Rank 4, 0.84: art-1187 chunk 2, version 1, deleted 17 Oct 2024. Below, the answer at 22:30, quoted from ranks 1 and 3.

notes.text: Thursday 22:30: the four chunks sent to the model

blocks.caption: Gwenno reran the question on Friday morning and drew what went to the model, by score: art-1187 chunk 1, 0.91; art-2290 chunk 1, 0.88; inv-0912 chunk 1, 0.86; art-1187 chunk 2, 0.84. The content system has no art-1187 at all. It holds art-2290 at version 2, corrected at 20:47 on Thursday, and inv-0912 in the investigations group only.

blocks.text: We held page five. Wylla's story ran at 06:00 as planned, and the councillor's solicitor hasn't called. Yet. The assistant is switched off until Monday. What do we change before it opens again?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your morgue came back from the dead. Your assistant doesn't search the content system; it searches its own index, a copy of the content system's text cut into chunks and embedded, kept beside it. A copy knows only what it's told. Most content systems can send a change feed: a stream of events, one for each document created, edited or deleted, often delivered as webhooks, calls to a web address you give them. Freshness lag is how long a change takes to reach the copy. Three questions for whoever built it. Which events does the pipeline act on, and what happens to the chunks when an article is deleted? When it stores a chunk, what does it keep beside the text and the vector? And when the assistant searches, whose eyes does it search with?

replies.author: u/morgue_pipes_gwenno
replies.text: Gwenno, I built it. The pipeline subscribes to two of the content system's webhooks, article created and article updated, and upserts the article's chunks: writes them if they're new, overwrites the ones with the same ID if not. There's no handler for deleted. Deletes were rare when I built it, and I meant to come back to it. Beside each chunk I keep the text, the vector, the article's ID and its version. Nothing about who may read it. The assistant searches as itself, across everything. Its dashboard says the lag is 90 seconds, because that's how long the events it handles take to arrive.

comments.author: u/fresh_enough_gerens
comments.text: Webhooks are a trap. Events go missing, arrive twice, arrive out of order, and before long you're debugging a tangle of moving parts for a search box. Throw the incremental pipeline away, the one that tries to follow each change as it happens, and do a nightly rebuild: build the whole index again from the content system every night at 02:00. Whatever's in the content system then is what's in the index, deleted articles are simply gone, and nothing can drift for more than a day. A nightly rebuild keeps it fresh enough. It's an archive, not a stock ticker.

replies.author: u/press_time_morvoren
replies.text: Our corrections go up at all hours. Thursday's, at 20:47, changed chair to vice-chair in a story about the same councillor.

replies.author: u/fresh_enough_gerens
replies.text: Then you live with one night of chair. Nobody gets sued over a vice-chair.

reply.prompt: The archive assistant is off until Monday. What should Gwenno change before it opens again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Feed the index from the change feed so deletes reach every chunk; store access groups on chunks, filter by asker; alert on lag.
options.part2: Gwenno spent the weekend on it. The pipeline now acts on every event the change feed sends: created, updated and deleted. Each event upserts by article ID and version, so a repeat overwrites the same chunks and a late, older version is skipped; a delete removes every chunk with that article's ID. Each chunk now carries its article's access groups, and the assistant searches with the asker's groups inside the search, then checks the four results against the content system before the model sees them. She replayed Thursday and Friday through it. art-1187's two chunks went, and the index held 7 chunks for the content system's 7. Thursday's question, asked as me at 22:30: art-2290 chunk 1 (0.88), art-0655 chunk 1 (0.83), art-2290 chunk 2 (0.80), art-2418 chunk 1 (0.77). Vice-chair, Harbour ward, the budget vote, and nothing else. Asked as Wylla, inv-0912 came second, as it should. When the embargo lifted at 06:00 on Friday, the draft became version 2 for the newsroom and reached my searches 90 seconds later. The lag alert is set at 5 minutes and now counts every change, deletes included. Gwenno says it's the part she trusts most, because for two years the old dashboard said 90 seconds.
options.senior: The index is a copy, and a copy needs both of the source's things: its changes and its rules. Drive it from every event in the change feed, with idempotent upserts keyed by document and version and deletes that reach every chunk; store each chunk's access groups and filter by the asker's inside the search, with a check against the source as a backstop; and measure lag from the source's side, so a change the pipeline ignores shows up as lag instead of hiding.

options.text: Drop the incremental pipeline and rebuild the whole index from the content system every night at 02:00, so nothing is a day old.
options.verdict: Fresh by morning, open to all
options.part2: Gwenno replaced the pipeline with a rebuild at 02:00 every night, and replayed Thursday through it before switching it on. At 22:30 art-1187 was gone, and so was the draft, which didn't exist at the last rebuild. But the answer said Carnsew was elected chair of the harbour board: the index held art-2290 at version 1, and the 20:47 correction was waiting for the next rebuild. The oldest change not yet in the index was 4 h 18 min old, the draft created at 18:12. Then she moved the clock to Friday 03:10, after the rebuild, and asked as me. inv-0912 chunk 1 came second, at 0.86. The rebuild had copied Wylla's embargoed draft in with everything else, with nothing to say who may read it, and the morning reporters start at 03:00. At 06:10, after the embargo lifted, the index still held the draft's old groups.
options.senior: A nightly rebuild removes deleted documents by accident and makes every other change wait up to a day. It does nothing for permissions: it copies drafts in with no record of who may read them. Rebuild when the embedding model changes or to recover, not to stay fresh.

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt telling the assistant never to use retracted articles or embargoed drafts, and to refuse if asked.
options.part2: Gwenno added the line and replayed Thursday at 22:30. The same four chunks went to the model: art-1187 chunk 1 (0.91), art-2290 chunk 1 (0.88), inv-0912 chunk 1 (0.86), art-1187 chunk 2 (0.84). Nothing in them said retracted or embargoed. The article that could have said so is deleted, and its chunks are just sentences; the draft's chunk is a sentence too, with no group beside it. The answer was word for word the same. Asked straight out whether the councillor had met the dredging firm, the assistant said yes, on 3 September.
options.senior: A model can only follow a rule about information it can recognise, and once a chunk is in its context, it has already been handed over. The system prompt is not access control. Keep what the asker may not see out of the search, and keep deleted text out of the index.

options.text: Split the index in two, one for the newsroom and one for investigations, each searchable only by its own desk's staff accounts.
options.part2: Gwenno split the index: a newsroom index for everyone, and an investigations index for Wylla's desk holding its drafts plus a copy of every newsroom article, because investigations staff read those too. The draft stopped reaching me. But both indexes were fed by the same pipeline, and it still had no handler for deleted. Replaying Thursday at 22:30, art-1187 chunk 1 came first again, at 0.91, and chunk 2 third. The two indexes held 16 chunks between them, 7 of them twice. When the embargo lifted, the draft's chunks had to move from one index to the other, and Gwenno started a list of which desk could read what.
options.senior: Separate indexes are real walls and simple to reason about while groups are few and fixed. Every shared document is stored once per group that may read it, a change of access becomes a move between indexes, and it does nothing for deletes. Access groups stored on each chunk scale further.

sim.title: Replay Thursday night through the index
sim.lede: You're Gwenno on Friday morning, replaying the night. There is no real model. The sim holds six documents from the content system, each with its versions, access groups, chunks and a stated score for the question about Councillor Carnsew, and the changes between them: art-1187 deleted on 17 Oct 2024 at 16:05; the draft inv-0912 created on Thursday at 18:12, investigations only; art-2290 corrected at 20:47; and the embargo lifted at 06:00 on Friday, when the draft becomes version 2 for the newsroom. Pick when, how the index is fed, how access is handled and who is asking. The change feed delivers each change 90 seconds after it happens; as now, it ignores deletes. The nightly rebuild copies the content system at 02:00, and the one-off load is the copy of 2 April 2024. The assistant sends the top 4 chunks by score. The lag alert fires above 5 minutes.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open at Thursday 18:00, as now: 7 chunks in the index for 5 in the content system, and the oldest change not yet in the index is 721 d 1 h 55 min old. Move to 22:30: art-1187 chunk 1 (0.91) and inv-0912 chunk 1 (0.86) are both among the four sent. Try the system prompt line. Switch to the change feed with deletes, then filter by access groups, and ask as each desk. Go back to as now with the filter and the check: 2 sent. Try a separate index per desk. Try the nightly rebuild at 22:30, at 03:10 and at 06:10, and the one-off load. Last, on the change feed, deliver the 20:47 edit twice.

explain.oneLine: Nothing came back from the dead. The assistant searched its own copy of the content system, the copy never heard about the delete, and it never knew who was allowed to read what.

steps.title: The index is a copy.
steps.text: The assistant never searches the content system. It searches an index built from it: chunks, their vectors, and whatever else the pipeline chose to keep. Dead Letter's newspaper morgue case made the same point about a word index: a search index is a copy, as fresh as whatever keeps it in step. Gwenno's pipeline acted on two webhooks, created and updated. When art-1187 was deleted on 17 October 2024 at 16:05, the content system sent an event nobody handled, and the article's two chunks stayed, scoring 0.91 and 0.84 for any question about Carnsew.

steps.title: Drive the index from every change, and make repeats harmless.
steps.text: Feed the index from the source's change feed: webhooks, or change data capture, which reads the database's own log so even changes no app announces are seen. Each event names the document, its version and what happened. Upsert the chunks keyed by document ID and version, and the write is idempotent: a repeated event overwrites the same chunks, and a late, older version is skipped because the index already holds a newer one. On an edit, chunk and re-embed the new version. If the number of chunks changes, delete the old ones first, or a leftover chunk from the old version lingers.

steps.title: A delete must reach every chunk.
steps.text: One article becomes several chunks, so give each a structured ID such as art-1187#1 and keep the article ID in its metadata; a delete then removes every chunk by that ID or by a metadata filter. A delete is an event to pass on, not an absence: like Dead Letter's tombstones, it has to reach every copy, and a copy that never hears it keeps the old text.

steps.title: Measure the lag from the source's side, and plan the big rebuild.
steps.text: Freshness lag is the time from a change in the content system to the index reflecting it. Gwenno's dashboard measured only the events the pipeline handled, so it said 90 seconds while the oldest change not in the index, the delete, was 721 d 6 h 25 min old at 22:30. Count every kind of change, alert above a threshold such as 5 minutes, and run a periodic reconciliation that compares document IDs and versions on both sides. When the embedding model changes, every vector must be computed again: re-index into a new index beside the old one and switch over when it's full, Dead Letter's expand and contract.

steps.title: Retrieval must respect permissions, and the prompt can't do it.
steps.text: Store each chunk's access groups, and have the search run as the person asking: filter by their groups inside the search, as this season's vault case filtered inside the index rather than after it, so the top 4 is filled with what they may read. Then check each result against the content system before it reaches the model, which catches a document deleted or restricted since the index last heard. A line in the system prompt changes no chunk: by the time the model reads it, the draft is already in its context.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row, left to right: the content system, articles and drafts, sends events to the change feed worker, which handles create, edit and delete and upserts by ID and version into the index, which keeps chunks, vectors, version and groups. Bottom row, right to left: the index answers a query from the search, which runs as the asker and filters by groups inside the search; its top 4 go to the check, which asks the content system whether each is still live and allowed; what passes goes to the model.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Monday. Every created, updated and deleted event reaches the index within about 90 seconds, keyed by article ID and version, and every chunk keeps its access groups. The search runs with the asker's groups, and the check asks the content system about each of the top 4 before the model sees it. Replayed for Thursday at 22:30 as the night desk: art-2290 (0.88), art-0655 (0.83), art-2290 (0.80), art-2418 (0.77).

fix.title: The fix: every change, every chunk, and the asker's groups
fix.text: Act on every event the content system's change feed sends: created, updated, deleted, and a change of access groups, which is an update too. Upsert chunks keyed by article ID and version, so repeats and late events can't do harm; on an edit, re-chunk and re-embed; on a delete, remove every chunk with that article's ID. Store each chunk's access groups, filter by the asker's groups inside the search, and check the results against the content system before the model sees them. Measure freshness lag from the content system's side for every kind of change, alert above 5 minutes, and reconcile IDs and versions on a schedule. Rebuild the whole index only when the embedding model changes, beside the old one.

limits: A change feed can drop an event. Idempotent upserts make repeats harmless, but a dropped event is silent until something compares the two sides, so the reconciliation job is part of the fix, not an extra.

The check against the content system costs a lookup for each result, and if the content system is down the assistant has to refuse rather than guess. The filter alone is only as current as the groups the feed last delivered.
Removing chunks from the index doesn't remove the text from logs, caches, backups or answers already given. A removal after a legal complaint has to reach those too.

head: How the index is kept
Good
Bad
rows: Simple, and nothing to run afterwards.
Frozen: at 22:30, 5 of the content system's 7 chunks missing and art-1187 still there.
Deleted documents vanish at the next 02:00. One simple job.
Up to a day behind (4 h 18 min at 22:30), copies drafts with no groups, re-embeds everything each night.
Change feed, creates and edits only (as now)
Deletes never arrive: the oldest change not in the index was 721 days old.
Change feed with deletes, groups on every chunk
Everything within 90 seconds, and search runs as the asker.
More moving parts: versions, repeats, reconciliation and a check against the source.
Real walls, simple while groups are few.
7 of 16 chunks stored twice, access changes become moves, deletes untouched.
A line in the system prompt
Changes no chunk: the same four reach the model.

explain.seniorTake: A RAG index is a copy of your sources, and a copy needs two things the source already has: its changes and its rules. Feed it from the source's change stream, all of it, with upserts keyed by document and version and deletes that reach every chunk. Measure lag from the source's side and alert on it, and reconcile now and then, because events go missing. Store who may read each chunk so the search runs as the person asking, and check again before the model sees anything. Keep full rebuilds for model changes and recovery. And never ask a model to keep a secret it has already been handed.

realWorld.title: Pinecone: an upsert overwrites by ID
realWorld.text: Pinecone's documentation, read today, says: "If a record ID already exists, upserting overwrites the entire record." That is what makes a repeated event harmless when the ID is stable, and why the ID should carry the document and the chunk.

realWorld.title: Pinecone: delete by ID or by metadata filter
realWorld.text: Its delete page says "deleting by ID is the most efficient way to remove specific records from a namespace", and: "To delete records from a namespace based on their metadata values, pass a metadata filter expression to the delete operation."

realWorld.title: Pinecone: chunks of one document
realWorld.text: Its data modeling guide recommends structured record IDs with a prefix for the parent document and a chunk number, and when a document's chunks change in number or order, the recommended approach is to "first delete all chunks using a metadata filter" before writing the new ones.

realWorld.title: Azure AI Search: the security filter pattern
realWorld.text: Microsoft's page describes a filter that "trims search results based on a string containing a group or user identity", stored in a field on each document. It warns: "There's no authentication or authorization through the security principal." Instead, "document-level authorization is enforced by applying the security filter to every query."

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM08:2025, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
realWorld.text: The entry warns: "Inadequate or misaligned access controls can lead to unauthorized access to embeddings containing sensitive information." Its first prevention step: "Implement fine-grained access controls and permission-aware vector and embedding stores."

realWorld.title: Debezium: change data capture that sees deletes
realWorld.text: Debezium, an open-source change data capture tool, lists among its features that it "Ensures that all data changes are captured" and "Can capture deletes": reading the database's log, rather than waiting for an app to announce each change.

asked: How do you keep a RAG index in sync with its sources?
How do you make retrieval respect permissions?
What happens to the index when a document is deleted?
interview.answer: I treat the index as a copy and drive it from the source's change feed, webhooks or change data capture, never a one-off load, and not a nightly rebuild if freshness matters. Every event carries the document ID and version, and I upsert chunks keyed by both, so repeats are harmless and an older version never overwrites a newer one; edits are re-chunked and re-embedded. A delete removes every chunk, by structured ID prefix or a metadata filter on the document ID, and I remember backups and caches too. I measure freshness lag from the source's side for every kind of change, alert on it, and reconcile IDs and versions on a schedule. For permissions, each chunk stores its access groups, the search filters by the asker's groups inside the query so the top-k fills with allowed chunks, and I check the results against the source before the model sees them. I never rely on the prompt to hide anything. When the embedding model changes, I build a new index beside the old one and switch over.

terms.def: The journalist in charge of a newspaper overnight, deciding what goes on each page before press time. Morvoren is the Gullstone Herald's.
The night editor and the staff working with her overnight. In the content system they are in the newsroom group.
The deadline when the pages go to the printing press. At the Herald it is 23:15.
The program where the Herald writes, edits and publishes every article and keeps drafts, each with versions and access groups. The assistant's index is built from it.
The Herald's RAG assistant: it searches an index built from the morgue and the content system and sends the top 4 chunks to a model, which writes the answer.
An elected member of a local council. Hedley Carnsew represents Harbour ward.
An area of a town that elects its own councillor or councillors.
The body that runs a town's harbour. Councillors often sit on it.
Digging silt from the floor of a harbour to keep it deep enough for boats, usually done by a contractor.
A public list where councillors record jobs, gifts, property and meetings that could affect their decisions.
A newspaper withdrawing an article it no longer stands by, usually with a correction or an apology. The Herald retracted art-1187 and deleted it on 17 October 2024.
A formal objection, usually from a lawyer, that an article unlawfully harms someone, often with a demand that it be removed.
An agreement that a story may not be published or acted on before a set time. inv-0912 was embargoed until 06:00 on Friday.
The reporters working on long investigations. Their drafts sit in the investigations group, which the night desk isn't in.
An article being written and not yet published.
An edit that fixes a published mistake. art-2290's, at 20:47 on Thursday, changed chair to vice-chair and made version 2.
A named group of staff, such as newsroom or investigations, allowed to open a document. Each article and draft in the content system lists its groups.
A numbered state of a document. Each edit, and each change to its access groups, makes a new version, such as art-2290 v2 or inv-0912 v2.
The searchable copy a RAG system builds from its sources: chunks, their vectors and any metadata kept beside them. It knows only what its pipeline tells it.
The code that takes documents from their source, chunks and embeds them and writes them to the index, then keeps the index in step as the source changes.
Copying every document into the index once. The Herald's ran on 2 April 2024 at 03:00; anything after needs something else to reach the index.
A stream of events from a source, one for each document created, edited or deleted, so other systems can follow its changes.
A call a system makes to a web address you give it whenever an event happens, such as article updated. A common way to deliver a change feed.
Reading a database's own log of changes to produce a change feed, so every insert, update and delete is seen, including ones no app announces.
An open-source change data capture tool that reads databases' change logs and turns every row change into an event.
How long a change in the source takes to reach the index. Measured from the source's side, it counts every kind of change, deletes included.
An alarm that fires when freshness lag passes a threshold. The fix sets it at 5 minutes.
Update or insert: write a record if its ID is new, or overwrite the record with that ID if it exists.
Giving the same result whether done once or many times. An upsert keyed by document ID and version is, so a repeated event does no harm.
Building the whole index again from the source every night, here at 02:00. Deleted documents vanish at the next rebuild; any later change waits for the one after.
A chunk in the index from an older version of its document than the source now holds.
A scheduled job that compares the document IDs and versions in the index with the source's and repairs any difference, catching events the feed dropped.
Building a whole new index from the sources, for example when the embedding model changes and every vector must be computed again.
Retrieval that returns only chunks the person asking may read, using access groups stored with each chunk and filtered inside the search.
Asking the content system, for each result, whether its document still exists and the asker may still read it, before the model sees it.
Giving each group its own index holding only what it may read. Simple walls, but a document several groups may read is stored several times.
A hosted vector database.
One stored item in Pinecone: an ID, a vector and optional metadata. A chunk is usually one record.
A partition of a Pinecone index. Reads, writes and deletes go to one namespace at a time.
Microsoft's hosted search service, with keyword, vector and hybrid search.
Azure AI Search's pattern for document-level permissions: a field of group or user IDs on each document, and a filter on that field in every query.
A user or group that permissions are given to, identified by an ID string.
OWASP's list of the ten most important security risks for apps built on large language models. The 2025 edition lists vector and embedding weaknesses as LLM08.
The 2025 OWASP entry on vector and embedding weaknesses: how stored vectors and the retrieval around them can leak information or be tampered with.
Information about an identifiable living person, as GDPR defines it, such as a name with a salary.
An assistant that answers staff questions about pay, leave and policies from the company's HR documents.
Removing other people's access to a file that was shared with them.
The similarity score the sim gives each chunk for the question about Carnsew, fixed in advance. Higher scores rank first.

terms.term: Oldest change not yet in the index (sim)
terms.def: The sim's lag figure: how long ago the earliest change the index doesn't yet reflect happened, or none when the index is up to date.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that answers from shared documents: an HR assistant, a policy bot, a sales assistant over a shared drive. A common incident: an HR assistant answers a question about pay from a salary spreadsheet a manager had shared with the wrong group and then unshared, because the index copied the sheet's chunks while it was shared and never stored who could read them. Ask three things. Which change events does the ingestion act on: created, edited, deleted, and a change of sharing or groups? What does each chunk carry beside its text and vector: the document ID, the version, the access groups? And who does the search run as? The usual fix is access groups stored on every chunk, a filter on the asker's groups inside the search at query time, a check against the source before the model sees a result, and a lag alert that counts every kind of change. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, an assistant that searches as itself works around Annex A 5.15 (access control), and chunks left behind after a delete work against 8.10 (information deletion); where the documents hold personal data, a GDPR Article 17 erasure request has to reach every chunk, cache and backup of it too. Build the groups on chunks, the delete handling and the lag alert in from the first version rather than before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant answers customers from the help centre through RAG. Last month the team removed a help article describing a refund policy you no longer offer, yet the assistant still quotes it, with a link that now returns a page not found error. The ingestion job listens for article published and article updated events. What is happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The index is a copy that never received the delete, so the article's chunks are still in it
Handle deletes by removing every chunk of the document, by its ID or a metadata filter
Measure freshness lag for every kind of change from the source's side, and reconcile the index against the source on a schedule

recall.model: The index is a copy of the help centre, and it never received the delete: the job only acts on published and updated events, so when the article was removed nothing touched its chunks, which are still in the index and still score well for refund questions. Subscribe to the delete event and handle it by removing every chunk of that article, by a structured ID prefix or a metadata filter on the article ID. Then replay or reconcile: compare the index's article IDs and versions with the help centre's, remove what no longer exists, and keep doing that on a schedule, because a feed can drop events. Finally, measure freshness lag from the help centre's side for every kind of change, deletes included, with a lag alert, so a change the job ignores shows up instead of hiding behind a healthy dashboard.

recall.prompt: A RAG assistant serves staff with different permissions over the same documents. Where should the rule about who may see a document be enforced?
options: In the system prompt, by telling the model which documents this user must not use
Inside the search, by filtering on access groups stored with each chunk, then checking the results against the source before the model sees them
After the answer, by asking a second model whether the answer leaks anything the user shouldn't see
In the user interface, by hiding the links to documents the user can't open
recall.why: Only the search decides what reaches the model. Filtering on each chunk's access groups inside the search keeps forbidden chunks out of the context and fills the top-k with allowed ones, and a check against the source catches anything deleted or restricted since the index last heard. A prompt rule or a second model acts after the text has already been handed over, and hiding links leaves the words in the answer.

recall.prompt: You're designing ingestion for a RAG assistant over a company wiki of 200,000 pages, edited all day. Pages can be edited, removed, or moved between spaces with different permissions, and the team plans to switch embedding models next year. Outline how the index stays in step with the wiki.

keyIdeas.idea: Drive ingestion from a change feed (webhooks or change data capture), not a one-off load or nightly rebuild
Idempotent upserts keyed by page ID and version; re-chunk and re-embed on edit; a delete removes every chunk
Store access groups with each chunk and filter by the asker's groups inside the search; a permission move is an update
When the embedding model changes, build a new index beside the old one and switch over when it's full

recall.model: I'd drive ingestion from the wiki's change feed, webhooks or change data capture, rather than a one-off load or a nightly rebuild, because pages change all day. Every event carries the page ID and version; I upsert chunks keyed by both, so the writes are idempotent, a repeated event does nothing and an older version never overwrites a newer one. An edit is re-chunked and re-embedded, and a removal deletes every chunk of the page by its ID. Each chunk stores the page's access groups, and the search filters by the asker's groups inside the search, so a move between spaces is just an update that rewrites the groups. I'd measure freshness lag from the wiki's side, alert on it, and reconcile IDs and versions nightly. For the embedding model change, I'd build a new index beside the old one, fill it while the old one serves, and switch over with an alias when it's complete.

recall.prompt: Your change feed delivers 'doc-88 version 5 updated' twice, and then a delayed 'doc-88 version 4 updated'. The index upserts chunks keyed by document ID and version, and skips a version older than the one it holds. What does the index hold for doc-88 afterwards?
options: Version 4's chunks, because that event arrived last
Two copies of version 5's chunks and one copy of version 4's
Version 5's chunks, once; the late version 4 is skipped
Nothing, because conflicting events cancel each other out
recall.why: An upsert keyed by the document ID overwrites the same chunks, so the second delivery of version 5 changes nothing, and because the index compares versions, the late version 4 is older than the stored version 5 and is skipped. That's what makes the writes idempotent and safe against events that arrive twice or out of order.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Thank you all. The pipeline now acts on created, updated and deleted events, every chunk carries its access groups, and the assistant checks every result against the content system. The lag alert has been quiet since October. In January our legal desk restricted an old article about a harbour landlord to the legal group while a complaint is looked at; nobody touched the text. Since then every question about the harbour comes back with three chunks instead of four, and Gwenno's logs show the check dropping that article's chunks about forty times a day. The content system lists the restriction as a permissions changed event.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the check keep dropping that article's chunks, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The pipeline doesn't act on that event type, so the chunks in the index still carry the old groups
Treat a change of access as an update: rewrite the chunks' groups as a new version, even with no text edit
The check is a backstop: count its drops and alert on them as a sign the index has drifted, and reconcile groups too

coldCase.model: The pipeline handles created, updated and deleted, but a restriction arrives as a different event type, and it doesn't handle that one, so the article's chunks still carry the old groups: newsroom. The filter trusts those old groups and lets the chunks into the top 4, and the check, asking the content system, sees legal only and drops them, which is why you get three chunks. Treat a change of access as an update: when the groups change, write a new version of the article's chunks with the new groups, even though the text is the same. Then reconcile groups as well as IDs and versions, and count the check's drops: the check is a backstop, and a steady stream of drops means the index has drifted from the source. Put an alert on that count, the way the lag alert watches time.
